sweep_summary: Thai (thai1261) is in the catalog as fixed-dominant final (final stress), domain word and phrase together on Noss 1964:31 (phrase-level rule). Of the 23 works with stress in the title, 9 previously unheld papers were found as full open scans on SEALang SALA (sealang.net/sala; expired TLS certificate, downloaded by automated download -k) and scanned at 300 dpi one page at a time: Peyasantiwong 1986 'Stress in Thai' (word-level: disyllables unstressed-stressed, final full stress in every 3+-syllable word, weak vs reduced non-final syllables by CV? shape; exceptions reduplications/doublets and separable compounds), Wong-opasi 1992 (primary stress on the last syllable of the word at the lexical level and of the phrase postlexically; final syllable heavy by position), Tumtavitikul 1997/1998 (same paper twice: last syllable always primary, right-headed feet and word tree, weight-based secondary stress suppressed in casual speech), Theraphan 1984 (rhythm paper, but states 'fixed word stress, such as Thai, where stress always falls on the last syllable of a word'), Gandour-Potisuk-Harper 1996 (compound-initial syllable unstressed; vowel length neutralized when unstressed), Noss 1972 (phrase rhythm, explicitly not stress), Gandour-Potisuk-Perkins 1997 (reiterant-speech method, silent), Tumtavitikul 2001 (verse metrics, restates right-headed word structure). Six Glottolog entries are duplicates (editor-as-author or double listing). Cooper et al. 1985 is an English study (mis-linked); Sarmah et al. 2011 is Thai English. Bennett 1995 dissertation is campus-restricted at IDEALS (abstract read: right-headed iambic feet; the open 1994 SLS article is already held). Not located anywhere open: Kroll 1956, Gillette 1955, Gsell 1979, Gsell n.d., Abramson 1979 (medium/low priority). Extras found via Crossref and downloaded open: Kaland et al. 2026 (Speech Prosody; stress recall; summarises Sirintranon & Hsieh 2024 TLR and Maluleem & Pittayaporn 2025 Word Structure, both paywalled) and Domrongchareon & Pittayaporn 2024; Potisuk et al. 1996 Phonetica abstract (compounds weak-strong, duration the main cue). Every source read agrees on final primary stress; nothing contradicts the classification. Best new statement: Peyasantiwong 1986:222-223, 226 — an explicit word-level final-stress rule that supersedes Noss 1964's phrase-level rule as the deciding word-stress citation and supports moving the domain from word and phrase together to word (secondary stress should stay a weight-dependent note, not a fixed string). all discovery went through SALA, Crossref, IDEALS, ISCA and archive.org/Open Library APIs.

new_statements.reading: An explicit word-level statement by a native-speaker linguist in a paper devoted to Thai word stress (sentence stress is deferred, p.212): polysyllabic words carry full (primary) stress on the final syllable in every case; non-final syllables are weak if underlyingly CV? and reduced otherwise (p.227 extends the rule to words of four or more syllables; n.2 p.228: word-final syllables are always stressed). Exceptions are reduplications/doublets and separable (non-institutionalized) compounds, whose members keep normal stress. This is the fixed: final syllable rule already in the catalog (final stress), now stated for the word rather than Noss's phonemic phrase; it agrees with Bennett 1994:44-45, Wong-opasi 1992:462 (final stress at both the word and the phrase level), Tumtavitikul 1998:63-66 and Theraphan 1984:4, so the domain can move from word and phrase together to word. Secondary stress is weight/shape-dependent (Peyasantiwong's 'reduced' vs 'weak'; Tumtavitikul's heavy non-final syllables), not fixed-positional.

new_statements.quote: Following Hayes 1994, I take stress to be abstract, realized structurally on the head syllables of prosodic constituents. The exponents of stress in Thai and Kayah Li are two syllable weight and tonality, two binary oppositions (which accounts for the lack of multiple stress levels). The close association of syllable weight with foot headship, plus a consistent pattern of metrical right-headedness, derives iambic foot structure, and forms the basis for the frequent distinction between major syllables and minor syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Abstract only: stress is realized on foot heads; feet are right-headed (iambic), and heavy syllables are foot heads while light (minor) syllables are unstressed, so the final (always heavy) syllable of a word is prominent and non-final heavy syllables also carry foot-head prominence. Speech style (hyper- vs hypo-articulated) changes how much foot structure is built.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Standard Thai (chs.3-4) is analysed with right-headed (iambic) metrical feet and right-headed prosodic words: the stressed syllable is the head, i.e. the final syllable of the foot and of the prosodic word, which for a polysyllabic word means final stress; stress is realised not by pitch/duration/loudness levels but by syllable weight and full tonality (head syllables are heavy and carry a lexical tone, non-head 'minor' syllables are light and toneless), so Thai distinguishes only stressed vs unstressed syllables. This is my reading of the abstract + ch.1 + section titles; the constraint rankings and the Thai data (pp.42-97) could not be read.

tone_statements.quote: It is usual to count the number of tones in the tone system under investigation by considering only the 12 slots of the smooth syllables. Thus, in Standard Thai there are five tones. The variants that occur in checked syllables are each analysed as an allotone of one of the tones in smooth syllables on the basis of phonetic similarity. ... Standard Thai therefore has five tones: rising, mid, low, falling, and high. The rising and mid tones only occur in smooth syllables. The falling and high tones occur in the smooth syllables as well as, respectively, in the long and the short checked syllables. The low tone occurs in all three types of syllables: smooth, long checked, and short checked.

sources.quote: Thai is a tone language. In a tone language, every syllable or word may have a distinctive pitch pattern as part of its phonemic structure. Thai has five contrastive pitch patterns, or lexical tones, traditionally labeled mid, low, falling, high, and rising (Gandour 1975). The primary acoustic correlate of tone is generally considered to be F0 states and movements. In prepausal position in Thai, the mid tone can be described as mid level with a final drop, low tone as low falling, falling tone as high falling, high tone as high rising, and rising tone as low rising (see Abramson 1962, 1976 for acoustical description of Thai tones).

sources.quote: Thai is traditionally viewed as having five phonemic tones. The maximum five-way differentiation can appear only on syllables ending in diphthongs, long vowels, or nasal consonants. sources.quote: Central Thai has five lexically contrastive tones: mid, low, high, falling, and rising (Haas, 1956; Henderson, 1949; Abramson, 1962). The mid, high, and low tones are static or level; their F0 trajectories are relatively flat. In contrast, the falling and rising tones are contour or dynamic tones; during these tones F0 changes direction sharply (Abramson, 1962). A sixth tone, a high checked tone with some glottal constriction toward the end, has been described by Noss (1964). It would appear, however, that in a grammar of Thai that does not require an autonomous phonology, this tone should be treated as a predictable variant of the high tone, thus leaving a system of only five tones. This view is accepted here. [...] any syllable ending with a stop consonant normally takes only two different tones, though exceptions are found in a few loan words. [p. 7] The domain of the tone is the syllable. [p. 8] Nevertheless, sentence intonation does not normally interfere with the tonal distinctions, although under certain conditions -- for example, weak stress in Thai -- certain tonal contrasts will collapse (Noss, 1964:28; Hiranburana, 1972). tone.quote: It is usual to count the number of tones in the tone system under investigation by considering only the 12 slots of the smooth syllables. Thus, in Standard Thai there are five tones. The variants that occur in checked syllables are each analysed as an allotone of one of the tones in smooth syllables on the basis of phonetic similarity. ... Standard Thai therefore has five tones: rising, mid, low, falling, and high. The rising and mid tones only occur in smooth syllables. The falling and high tones occur in the smooth syllables as well as, respectively, in the long and the short checked syllables. The low tone occurs in all three types of syllables: smooth, long checked, and short checked.
